newsitem.title: USA: Dollar rises in thin trade after French audit.
newsitem.headline: Dollar rises in thin trade after French audit.

text.p: The dollar crept higher in extremely light trade on Monday, helped in part by a French public sector audit which fuelled speculation that Europe's planned single currency will be weak.

The audit of French public finances revealed on Monday that France's budget deficit was running at 3.5 percent to 3.7 percent of gross domestic product for 1997 -- well above the 3.0 percent target mandated by the Maastricht treaty for countries launching the single currency in 1999.

In the aftermath of the audit, the French government announced it would raise taxes on big business and cut spending in order to reduce the deficit ratio and help it get closer to the 3.0 percent goal.
These fiscal measures fuelled expectations that Europe's currency plan would go ahead on schedule, but also raised fears that the single currency, known as the euro, would be a weak unit.

Ernst Welteke, a council member of Germany's central bank, reinforced these expectations when he said he expected a timely start to monetary union, including both France and Germany, despite the French government's inability to meet the 3.0 percent target.

"If you look at the French audit it still appears that the euro is going to be a weak currency and I think that's the reason the dollar came back," said Rob Sabia, vice president at ING Barings Capital Markets.
The dollar ended at 1.7960 German marks, up from 1.7925 late Friday. The dollar also rose to 116.15 Japanese yen from Friday's closing rate of 115.60.

On a day when activity in the major currencies was extremely light, the Indonesian rupiah fell victim to a speculative attack, plunging to an historic low of 2,665 against the dollar before staging a marginal recovery on central bank intervention.

Speculative selling has battered the Thai baht, Philippine peso, Malaysian ringgit and Singapore dollar in recent weeks and dealers said the rupiah's fall represented spillover from the markets of Indonesia's Southeast Asian neighbours.
Some traders attributed the dollar's strength against the yen to the persistent troubles plaguing these Asian currencies, but for the most part, dollar trading was quiet on Monday.

The Sea's Day holiday in Japan and caution ahead of Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's semiannual Humphrey-Hawkins testimony to Congress on Tuesday and Wednesday contributed to the subdued market, dealers said.
"We have Greenspan coming up and Japan was out on holiday which gives people an excuse to sit back and watch from the sidelines," said John Gariano, vice president at Sumitomo Bank New York.
In other trade, the dollar closed at 1.4750 Swiss francs, just down from 1.4755 on Friday, and rose to Canadian $1.3775 from C$1.3747. Sterling edged down slightly to $1.6787 from $1.6790.
